1:
Ellicott reads the opening word as a hinge of the kind Paul turns elsewhere at the end of a great passage, where the vision of future glory becomes an inspiring force giving life to the sober practical duties of the present. Henry takes the inference the same way: since our conversation is in heaven and we look for the Saviour to come from there, the believing hope of eternal life should make us steady, even and constant in our course. Robertson notes that longed for is a late and rare verbal adjective occurring here alone in the New Testament, and puts the exhortation in its situation, that they were tempted to defection and standing firm is difficult once a panic starts. Both Calvin and Gill are struck by the string of endearments and both insist on what they are not. Calvin says Paul insinuates himself into their affections by lovely and kind names dictated not by flattery but by sincere affection, delighted to see men gained through his own instrumentality persevering in the faith; Gill says they are given in the uprightness of his soul without any manner of flattery. Wesley reduces the charge to four words: so stand, as ye have done hitherto.

The two names then divide the commentators three ways. Barnes takes both for women, allowing that Syntyche is sometimes a man's name but holding that the next verse settles it, and reports the common supposition that they were deaconesses while denying there is certain evidence for it. Clarke inclines the other way, that Euodias was a woman and Syntyche a man, probably her husband, and that it is he whom Paul addresses as yokefellow immediately after. Ellicott corrects the spelling to Euodia, dismisses the many strange attempts to find symbolism in the names, and places them as women of note at a city where the gospel was first preached to women and the church first met in a woman's house. Robertson gives the etymologies, prosperous journey and pleasant acquaintance, both attested in the inscriptions, and runs through the guesses: that each woman had a congregation in her house, one Jewish and one Gentile; that they were ladies of rank; that in so pure a church even slight bickerings would make a real disturbance. Calvin doubts the quarrel altogether, since the words afford no sufficient ground for the conjecture and Paul honours them enough to call them his fellow-soldiers in the gospel.

The yokefellow has exercised conjecture longer still. Ellicott first softens the verb, since entreat is too strong for a word that properly means to ask a question and then to make a request as of right, and notes the opinion, as old as Clement of Alexandria, that Paul meant his own wife, which he thinks untenable against what Paul says elsewhere of his unmarried state. Gill dismisses the same reading on three grounds, that Paul had no wife, that the word is masculine, and that some take it for the proper name Syzygus. Calvin declines to argue about the gender but finds the argument of Erasmus excessively weak, since it infers a woman from the mention of women, as though Clement's name were not joined in the same breath. Robertson observes that the proposal of Lydia founders on a masculine vocative, that Lightfoot even suggested Epaphroditus, a curious turn since he carried the letter, and concludes that it matters little who the peacemaker was. Wesley alone names a candidate with a reason: Paul had many fellow-labourers but few yokefellows, and Silas had been his yokefellow at that very city. Clarke explains why women were needed for the work at all.
4:
Chrysostom begins with a contradiction to resolve, since Christ blessed those that mourn and pronounced woe on those that laugh, yet Paul commands rejoicing always. His answer distinguishes the objects: the woe falls on the laughter of this world, which arises from things present, and the blessing on those pricked at heart who mourn their own faults, so that this joy is not contrary to that grief but born out of it, the man who grieves for his sins and confesses them being the one who rejoices. Ellicott adds that the word is the ordinary classical form of farewell, meaning joy be with you, and that the verse resumes what was broken off before the digression; but the weight laid on it here, with the constant returns to joy throughout the letter, shows the strict sense was intended and the duty pressed. Robertson agrees the greeting sense is not in view, and hears the repeated imperative as emphasis kept up in spite of discouragements. Calvin fits it to the moment, that with dangers on every side the Philippians might have given way, overcome by grief or impatience, and Clarke reads the repetition as showing not merely the apostle's earnestness but that the thing was God's will.

Nobody is satisfied with the English word moderation. Gill runs through the versions and rejects one outright, since the Ethiopic gives authority, which by no means agrees when the thing meant lies in clemency rather than in exerting power to the uttermost. Barnes makes it restraint on the passions and general soberness of living, the underlying sense being what is fit or suitable. Clarke calls the range of the word very extensive, and borrows Macknight's definition entire: meekness under provocation, readiness to forgive injuries, equity in the management of business, candour in judging the characters and actions of others, sweetness of disposition, and the entire government of the passions. Ellicott defines it against strict duty, as the sense of what is seemly or equitable rather than what formal law requires, the thing the world gropes after when it speaks of good taste or right feeling or the spirit of a gentleman; Robertson simply borrows Matthew Arnold's phrase, sweet reasonableness. Calvin weighs two readings and prefers enduring all things with equanimity, not easily moved by injuries nor easily annoyed by adversity. Wesley presses the reach of it, that the roughest tempers are good-natured to some from natural sympathy, while a Christian must be so to all.

The command against care is at once qualified. Barnes denies it forbids all concern for worldly matters, since a man must preserve his property and provide for his family, and takes it rather of a confidence in God that frees the mind; Gill limits it the same way, saints being bound to care for their bodies and households. Ellicott hears in it an exact repetition of the Lord's own take no thought, and observes that one may sink below the anxiety in mere levity as well as rise above it by casting care on him who cares for us. Clarke states the practical case, that anxiety cannot change anything from bad to good but will infallibly injure the soul, and distinguishes prayer as solemn application from a sense of want from supplication as continuance in earnest prayer. Wesley makes the two incompatible outright, since carefulness and prayer cannot stand together, and blames a preposterous shame that stifles desires as too small or too great. On the peace that follows, Robertson takes the verb as garrisoning and pictures it as a sentinel mounting guard, Clarke as keeping the heart in a castle, and Calvin insists it is a promise and not, as some make it, a prayer.
8:
Barnes takes the list as a concession with a demand inside it. Paul assumes there are things admitted to be true and pure and good in the world which were never directly revealed, and his object is that the Christian should exhibit exactly those: not partial virtues, not one set of duties performed to the neglect of another, not punctuality in religious rites alongside neglect of the common laws of morality. Gill puts the same reach in a word, that whatever is really true is meant, even among the very heathens, as against falsehood and lying and hypocrisy. Robertson resists the temptation to make a source of it, holding that the six adjectives are old-fashioned and familiar words rather than borrowings from any philosophic catalogue of excellencies, Stoic or otherwise, and that without such ideals none can exist at all; he thinks them the more pertinent now that so much filth is flaunted before the world in books and magazines and moving-pictures under the name of realism. Clarke reads the whole as a refusal to let righteousness be sectional, so that they attend not to one branch of virtue but to everything that brings honour to God, good to their fellow creatures and credit to themselves.

On the individual words the readings diverge in interesting ways. Ellicott pairs them: truth is the inherent likeness to God who is Truth, and whatever is true is thereby venerable, claiming a share of the reverence due primarily to God; just is righteousness in act and word as tested against a declared will, while pure is righteousness in essence, in the thought that cannot be so tested and is holier still. Clarke glosses the second term as grave, decent and venerable, whatever becomes a man as man, as citizen and as Christian. Robertson notes that two of the six occur nowhere else in the New Testament, the one meaning winsome and the other fair-speaking. Wesley alone finds a structure, eight particulars in two rows of four, the first row naming the duty and the second its commendation, word answering to word — true in speech, honest in action, just towards others, pure towards ourselves — and asks what is more lovely than truth. Calvin reads the first term as nothing else than the integrity of a good conscience with its fruits, and then adds the requirement Paul does not think the rest sufficient without: that we endeavour to make ourselves agreeable to all, so far as may lawfully be done.

Pointing to himself as the pattern strikes several of them as the boldest thing in the chapter. Barnes observes that only the consciousness of a pure and upright life could make such counsel proper, and adds how few men there are who could urge others to imitate everything they have seen and heard of them. Robertson makes the same point as a rule for the office, that the preacher is the interpreter of the spiritual life and should be an example of it, and notes that the verb is the one for practice as a habit. Calvin turns it into a maxim about preaching, that the main thing in a public speaker is to speak not with his mouth merely but by his life, procuring authority for his doctrine by rectitude of living, which is what gives Paul the standing to exhort at all. Clarke separates the four verbs into their sources, what was learned from the preaching, received by faith as revelation, heard both publicly and in private and from other churches, and seen while he laboured among them. Ellicott marks the change in the closing promise, since to have the peace of God with us is much and to have the God of peace himself is more.
10:
The verb Paul uses for their revived care is a piece of poetry, and everyone reaches for the same season. Robertson traces it to Homer, to sprout or blossom again, and notes it is used transitively here, so that they caused their thinking of him to bloom afresh; Clarke calls it the reviviscence of flowers in spring that seemed dead through winter; Calvin borrows the figure from trees whose strength is drawn inward and lies concealed till the season turns; Wesley simply says, as a tree blossoms after the winter. Ellicott alone hears a note under the gladness, some hitherto disappointed expectation, since at Rome, the metropolis of universal concourse, Paul might have looked for earlier word than at Caesarea, where he was cut off from the European churches — though he adds the excuse at once rather than wound them with even the semblance of reproof. Barnes puts the same excuse plainly, that the delay was not neglect or inattention but the difficulty of communicating with him. Henry credits Paul with a grateful spirit, speaking of their kindness as though it were generous charity when it fell far short of a just debt.

Chrysostom turns the thanks into a doctrine of giving, that almsgiving was introduced not for the sake of the receivers but of the givers, since the givers make the greatest gain; and he reads Paul's praise as calculated both to keep those who had helped him from being lifted up with arrogance and to make them more zealous in well-doing. The word for contentment then draws a comparison nobody quite wants to make. Ellicott and Robertson both observe that it means self-sufficing and was the especial characteristic the Stoics claimed for their ideal wise man, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament; Ellicott allows the nobleness of it, so far as it means sitting loose to the things of the world, while marking where it turns inhuman. Wesley heads the comparison off in a line, that Paul was no Stoic but had strong passions, all of them devoted to God. Calvin locates the thing itself in the disposition, since no man can be poor in mind who is satisfied with the lot assigned him by God, saints not measuring sufficiency by abundance. Barnes adds that prosperity needs as much grace as adversity and perhaps more, since adversity at least does something of itself.

The verb for being instructed is stranger still, and three of them say so. Robertson explains that it is the word for initiating a man with secret rites, found only here in the New Testament, so that Paul draws his metaphor from the initiations of the pagan mysteries; Ellicott renders it I have learnt the secret and names the Eleusinian rites; Clarke keeps the same sense, that he was fully initiated into all the mysteries of poverty and want. Wesley notices the ascent of the four expressions, I have learned, I know, I am instructed, I can. On the last of these Gill refuses the unlimited reading, since Paul was not omnipotent and could not do all that Christ could, so the claim must be restrained to the matter in hand; Ellicott renders it as having strength rather than doing, and takes it in the context of bearing. Clarke and Ellicott agree besides that the name of Christ is absent from the best manuscripts. Calvin marks how carefully Paul looks in both directions at once, guarding against the suspicion that want had broken him and equally against the appearance of despising their gift, which would be not merely obstinacy but haughtiness.
15:
Robertson turns the accounting language into the point of the passage. The apostle speaks of an account opened in the matter of giving and receiving, credit and debit, and no other church opened one with him; Robertson observes that not even Antioch contributed anything, and that only later did Thessalonica and Beroea join Philippi in supporting the work at Corinth. Ellicott marks the naming of the church itself as emphatic, a way of pointing at the dignity of their exclusive position, and dates the reference to the departure from Macedonia for Athens and Corinth. Clarke says the same flatly, that having preached to them he went into Macedonia and received help from none of the churches he had founded but from them alone, nothing being offered him elsewhere. Calvin reads the sentence as an excuse rather than a boast, since a man who often receives may be thought too eager to receive; in clearing himself Paul praises them, and in praising them he modestly excuses the others — a caution Calvin turns on his readers, that we take heed lest the pious, seeing us too much inclined to receive, should on good grounds reckon us insatiable.

On the gifts sent to Thessalonica the commentators supply the working arrangement behind them. Clarke notes that while planting that church Paul supported himself partly by his own hands and partly by what came from Philippi, and adds the unflattering observation that the Thessalonians themselves contributed little to his maintenance. Ellicott makes the same point as a principle, that at Thessalonica and at Corinth, both rich and luxurious communities, Paul refused maintenance, and that what came from Philippi once and again was meant to supplement his own resources and not to supersede them. Robertson renders the phrase both once and twice. Gill and Barnes fix the sequence, that from Philippi he went to Thessalonica and stayed long enough to plant a flourishing church under much opposition. Paul then guards himself again, and Gill hears the disavowal as aimed at a particular class, since he was not like the false teachers who made merchandise of men, and sought not theirs but them. Barnes and Calvin both take the disclaimer at its word: the interest is not in the gift but in what the giving shows, Paul consulting their advantage rather than his own, so that what redounds is to their account.

The receipt Paul gives is deliberately excessive. Ellicott renders it more strongly than our version, I have all to the full and more than to the full, and notes that Paul is not content even with that but adds a third term, so that the exuberance of courtesy and gratitude is strongly marked. Gill thinks the fulness owing less to the size of the present than to the peace of his mind, a small gift being a fulness to him. Then the language turns sacrificial, and Clarke and Ellicott alike take the sweet smell as alluding to the offerings of the law, Ellicott adding that Paul at once explains his own metaphor by calling it a sacrifice acceptable and well-pleasing to God. On the promise that follows, Gill reports that the Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic read it as a wish rather than an assertion, and Calvin knows the same reading and prefers the other. Robertson keeps the commercial figure to the end, that God has an abundant treasure in glory and will repay them. Henry closes on the doxology, that it is a great condescension in God to own the relation of Father to sinners and allow us to use the word.
21:
The closing greeting is unusual for being general, and Barnes says so: Paul commonly names names at the end of a letter, particularly prominent members, and why none are specified here is not known; he suspects that no individual Roman Christians were personally known at Philippi. Barnes also distinguishes the two groups, taking the brethren with him to mean the ministers, on the suggestion that at Rome the ministers went by that general name, while the saints follow in the next verse. Clarke supplies the likely company from the other letters of the imprisonment, naming Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras, Luke and Demas; Ellicott gathers the same list from Colossians and Philemon but declines to say how many were present at this particular moment, noting only that they are marked off from the body of the church. Gill presses the word every, so that the salute takes in rich and poor, weaker and stronger believers, the common saints as well as the bishops and deacons. The greeting from Rome then names a group that startles all of them.

Robertson is careful about what the household means, not members of the imperial family but people attached to the establishment, a term covering slaves and freedmen and even the highest functionaries; he draws the long conclusion that the gospel works upward from the lower classes and had begun to undermine the throne, and sets the obscure prisoner against the emperor who would kill himself shortly after Paul was executed. Clarke keeps the wonder smaller and sharper, that if even some of Nero's slaves were converted it would be marvellous enough, and reports from Josephus that Poppaea was a worshipper of the true God, so that she may have put no hindrance in the way of servants who wished to believe. Ellicott brings evidence, following Lightfoot's comparison of the names greeted in Romans with sepulchral inscriptions of the imperial household, where many prove identical, and suggests the praetorian guard as the channel of access. Calvin calls it no common evidence of divine mercy that the gospel made its way into that sink of all crimes, holiness being rare in the courts of sovereigns, and rejects the guess that Seneca was among them, since he gave not the smallest evidence of it and was a senator besides.

The last verse is settled on textual grounds and the corpus agrees for once. Ellicott states the true reading to be with your spirit rather than with you all, the familiar form being the more ordinary kind of salutation, and observes that in one shape or another the benediction is the token in every epistle. Clarke lists the evidence: the word our is absent from many manuscripts and versions, and for all a long line of uncials reads Spirit, supported by the Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate and Old Latin, besides several of the Fathers. Gill has met the same variant in the Vulgate, the Ethiopic and the Alexandrian copy, and adds what the sentence was for, that the benediction written in Paul's own hand was the mark by which a letter of his was known to be genuine. Barnes turns to the note appended after it and is blunt about its standing, that the subscriptions carry no authority whatever, though he thinks this one correct, since the letter bears internal evidence of having been written from Rome and was doubtless carried by Epaphroditus; he notes that the subscriptions vary considerably among themselves.
